claims.claim: A lawsuit starts with two documents: a Summons and a Complaint.
claims.quote: a summons shall be directed to the defendant, signed by the clerk and issued under the seal of the court in which the action is pending
claims.note: The section mentions both documents but describes the summons in an already pending action. It does not establish that the two documents start the lawsuit.

claims.quote: (1) The title of the court in which the action is pending.
claims.note: This is a listed item of summons content.

claims.claim: The Summons gives a case number.
claims.note: The statute does not list a case number. The cited form was not provided for inspection.

claims.claim: The Summons tells you how long you have to respond.
claims.quote: (3) A direction that the defendant file with the court a written pleading in response to the complaint within 30 days after summons is served on the defendant.
claims.note: The required direction states the response period and when it begins.

claims.claim: A collection letter is not a lawsuit, even if it says it may become one.
claims.note: No source addressing collection letters or threatened litigation was provided.

claims.claim: A collection phone call is not a lawsuit, even if it says it may become one.
claims.note: No source addressing collection calls or threatened litigation was provided.

flags.text: A summons-content statute does not establish a two-document commencement rule for every California consumer debt matter. Its content requirements are also qualified by “Except as otherwise required by statute”.
SUM-100 is missing, and no supplied source addresses the status of collection letters or calls.
A reader who receives only one document could infer that no lawsuit is pending and disregard a response deadline.

result.summary: The statute supports the court-name and response-period claims. It does not verify the two-document commencement rule, the case-number claim, or the statements about collection communications.
